title: US Workforce AI Exposure
description: Share of US jobs with significant task overlap with current AI capabilities. Exposure measures what AI could automate, not what it has. High exposure does not equal displacement.
disclaimer: Exposure measures which tasks could be affected by AI, not which jobs will be lost. Sources use fundamentally different definitions of 'exposure' — from individual task overlap to full occupation-level capability mapping. The 23–93% range reflects these definitional differences, not measurement uncertainty. The weighted average is a mathematical summary, not a consensus estimate. Explore task-level detail in the [Task Visualizer](/task-visualizer).

sources.title: Future of Work Report: AI at Work
sources.excerpt: 55% of LinkedIn members hold jobs that stand to be impacted by generative AI. By 2030, the skills required for jobs will change by up to 65%.

sources.title: AI Adoption in America: Who, What, and Where
sources.publisher: Journal of Economics & Management Strategy (McElheran, Li, Brynjolfsson et al.)
sources.excerpt: Employment-weighted adoption was just over 18%. AI use in production was found in every sector of the economy. Manufacturing and information led at roughly 12% each. Based on the 2018 Annual Business Survey of 850,000 firms.

sources.title: The Potentially Large Effects of AI on Economic Growth
sources.excerpt: Roughly two-thirds of current jobs are exposed to some degree of AI automation; generative AI could substitute up to one-fourth of current work.

sources.title: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: AI and the Labour Market
sources.excerpt: 27% of jobs are in occupations at high risk of automation across OECD countries.

sources.title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
sources.excerpt: Almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, with advanced economies more affected.

sources.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs
sources.excerpt: ~80% of the US workforce could have at least 10% of their tasks affected by GPTs. Legal, accounting, and financial analysis are among the highest-exposure occupations.

sources.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
sources.excerpt: In about 40% of employment in exposed occupations, at least 50% of tasks will be replaceable. Average labor-cost savings ~25% from current tools, potentially 40% as systems improve.

sources.title: The Anthropic Economic Index: Economic Primitives
sources.excerpt: Computer/mathematical tasks account for ~33% of all Claude.ai conversations and ~50% of API traffic, indicating concentrated AI impact on tech-adjacent roles.

sources.title: The Labor Market Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: Stanford / World Bank (Hartley, Jolevski, Melo, Moore)
sources.excerpt: LLM adoption among U.S. workers increased from 30.1% to 38.3% between December 2024 and December 2025. Small effects on wages in exposed occupations; no significant effects on job openings or total jobs.

sources.title: AI exposure predicts unemployment risk
sources.excerpt: Workers in AI-exposed occupations face significantly higher unemployment risk.

sources.title: AI and jobs: A review of theory, estimates, and evidence
sources.excerpt: Productivity gains 20-60% in controlled RCTs, 15-30% in field experiments; AI exposure measures converge toward high-wage jobs being most exposed.

sources.title: New Work, New World 2026: How AI is Reshaping Work
sources.excerpt: 93% of all occupations analyzed have at least one task with significant AI exposure. Education task exposure jumped from 11% to 49% — a 4.5x increase. Based on reassessment of 18,000 tasks across 1,000 O*NET occupations.

sources.title: Measuring US workers' capacity to adapt to AI-driven job displacement
sources.excerpt: Administrative support occupations have lower adaptive capacity (0.360) combined with the highest AI exposure of any major occupation group (0.525).

sources.title: January 2026 US Labor Market Update: Jobs Mentioning AI Are Growing Amid Broader Hiring Weakness
sources.excerpt: 45% of data & analytics job postings mentioned AI, the highest among all sectors analyzed...software development, IT systems & solutions, and scientific research & development each mentioned AI 20% or more of the time

sources.title: Fault Lines
sources.excerpt: Many kinds of writing and editing jobs are among those most exposed, with over 70% of their core skills potentially affected. On the other end of the spectrum, healthcare and first responder jobs dominate the low end of the rankings.

sources.title: How Well Does Agent Development Reflect Real-World Work?
sources.publisher: Carnegie Mellon / Stanford (Wang, Neubig, Fried, Yang et al.)
sources.excerpt: Across all benchmarks, examples collectively cover a limited 56.5% of the domain taxonomy but a substantially broader 85.4% of the skill taxonomy.

sources.title: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion
sources.excerpt: In recent years, retail trade has the lowest share of tasks that have been automated — around 50% — whereas computers/electronics has the highest share — more than 85%.

sources.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
sources.excerpt: At the bottom end, 30% of workers have zero coverage, as their tasks appeared too infrequently in our data to meet the minimum threshold.

sources.title: Bridging the AI Skills Gap: Is Training Keeping Up?
sources.excerpt: With one in three job vacancies having high AI exposure, a significant share of jobs in OECD economies are influenced by the rise of AI. Only a small percentage of training courses currently deliver AI content.

sources.title: Generative AI and Firm Values
sources.excerpt: the overall Generative AI exposure of the tasks in all white-collar occupations is 40% versus 9% for blue-collar and service occupations

sources.title: Generative AI and Firm Values
sources.excerpt: 678 occupations having on average 23% of their tasks exposed to Generative AI

sources.title: Skills Exposure to AI
sources.excerpt: 17-36% of worker skills exposed at moderate-to-high AI capability level.

sources.title: Worker Preferences for Task Automation
sources.excerpt: Workers want 46% of their tasks automated; preferences vary by task type and worker characteristics.

sources.title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
sources.publisher: MIT / Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Project Iceberg)
sources.excerpt: Analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics skill taxonomies reveals that current AI systems can technically perform approximately 16 percent of classified labor tasks. The Iceberg Index for digital AI shows values averaging 11.7%—five times larger than the 2.2% Surface Index.

sources.title: Labor Market AI Exposure: What Do We Know?
sources.publisher: The Budget Lab at Yale (Gimbel, Kendall, Kulsakdinun)
sources.excerpt: AI exposure metrics broadly agree with each other, but that they disagree with each other more on highly exposed occupations. The key point of disagreement between different AI exposure metrics is in the magnitude of exposure, not whether an occupation is exposed.

sources.title: How Adaptable Are American Workers to AI-Induced Job Displacement?
sources.excerpt: We find a positive correlation (r = 0.502) between AI exposure and a novel measure of worker adaptive capacity to displacement. Higher-income, highly skilled workers in professional occupations typically possess characteristics that enable successful navigation of job transitions.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta / Duke University (Baslandze et al.)
sources.excerpt: Employment effects heterogeneous by firm size: large companies expect AI-driven workforce reductions while smaller firms anticipate modest employment growth. Compositional reallocation of labor both within and across firms, with routine clerical roles declining and skilled-technical roles increasing.

sources.title: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society
sources.excerpt: Transformative AI sharply expands what counts as codifiable -- and therefore transferable -- 'local knowledge,' in three main ways: it makes explicit knowledge more accessible to decision-makers, it increasingly extracts tacit know-how once embedded in human perception and practice, and it generates machine-native knowledge.

sources.title: State of AI in the Enterprise: The untapped edge
sources.excerpt: Despite high expectations for automation, 84% of companies have not redesigned jobs or the nature of work itself around AI capabilities.

sources.title: How Will AI Affect the US Labor Market?
sources.excerpt: In the US, AI can potentially automate tasks that account for 25% of all work hours, Briggs' team finds.

sources.title: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: January/February CPS Update
sources.excerpt: The share of workers in the lowest, middle, and highest occupational exposure groups stay stable. Even when specifically examining the unemployed population, there is no clear growth in exposure to generative AI.

sources.title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
sources.publisher: The Budget Lab at Yale (Gimbel, Kendall, Kulsakdinun)
sources.excerpt: The share of workers in the lowest, middle, and highest occupational exposure groups stay stable. Irrespective of the duration of unemployment, unemployed workers were in occupations where about 25 to 35 percent of tasks, on average, could be performed by generative AI. Both samples indicate that observed usage is more likely to be associated with automation than augmentation.

sources.title: How Will AI-driven Automation Actually Affect Jobs?
sources.publisher: Substack (Alex Imas, Soumitra Shukla — U of Chicago Booth)
sources.excerpt: Two jobs with identical exposure scores can have completely opposite displacement risks depending on whether their tasks are complements, whether demand for their output is elastic or inelastic, and the incentives of the firm to invest in automation.

sources.title: O-Ring Automation
sources.excerpt: Widely-used exposure indices, which aggregate task-level automation risk using linear formulas, will overstate displacement when tasks are complements. The relevant object is not average task exposure but the structure of bottlenecks and how automation reshapes worker time around them.

sources.title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
sources.excerpt: About 49% of jobs have seen at least a quarter of their tasks performed using Claude.

sources.title: Will Wired Belts Become the New Rust Belts? AI and the Emerging Geography of American Job Risk
sources.publisher: Digital Planet, The Fletcher School, Tufts University
sources.excerpt: There are 4.9 million 'tipping point' workers -- spanning 33 occupations that swing from <10% to >40% displacement in the next 2-5 years across the US.

sources.title: AI Quarterly Pulse Survey Q1 2026
sources.excerpt: 87% Upskilling/reskilling current workforce

sources.title: Generative AI and Occupational Entry Barriers: The Labor-Supply Channel of Technological Change
sources.excerpt: We define a binary automation exposure indicator that equals one for tasks in categories 4–5, i.e., more than 80 percent automatable. Under this definition, 4,107 tasks (21.3 percent) are classified as exposed. The mean PSS is about 0.11, implying that for the average occupation, GenAI expands the qualified labor pool by 10 percentage points of the workforce.

sources.title: How AI may reshape career pathways to better jobs
sources.excerpt: Some 15.6 million—or one-fifth of the nation's 70 million STARs—work in roles highly exposed to AI, meaning they reside in the top quartile of observed occupational task exposure among occupations.

sources.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Forecasting Research Institute (w/ Fed Chicago, Yale, Stanford, UPenn)
sources.excerpt: 69 economists assign 61.4% probability to moderate or rapid AI capability progress by 2030. In the rapid scenario, AI surpasses humans on most cognitive and physical tasks.

sources.title: Economists Once Dismissed the A.I. Job Threat, but Not Anymore
sources.excerpt: Most still do not see much evidence that A.I. is disrupting the job market. But they are starting to take seriously the possibility that it could someday soon.

sources.title: Complement or Substitute? How AI Increases the Demand for Human Skills
sources.excerpt: When AI demand doubles in a job ad, demand for complementary skills rises by 5%. Complementary effects are 1.7x larger than substitution effects. Based on 12 million US job vacancies 2018-2023.

sources.title: Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides: Preliminary Findings on AI Automation from Thousands of Worker Evaluations of Labor Market Tasks
sources.excerpt: AI models successfully complete tasks that take humans approximately 3-4 hours with about a 50% success rate, increasing to about 65% by 2025-Q3. Most text-based tasks projected to reach 80-95% AI success by 2029. 62.6% of O*NET tasks classified as having at least 10% LLM time-savings potential. Based on 17,205 expert evaluations across 3,000+ O*NET tasks and 40+ LLMs.

sources.title: AI Adoption by Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
sources.publisher: OECD (Calvino, Bianchini, Lane, Montegu, Verger, Ancheva)
sources.excerpt: Around a quarter of workers in OECD Member countries are exposed to generative AI, meaning 20% of their job tasks could be done at least 50% faster with the help of generative AI.

sources.title: Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities
sources.publisher: MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (Cai, YeckehZaare, Sun et al.)
sources.excerpt: 92% of AI applications map to only 6.8% of 39,603 classified work activities. AI apps grew 6x from 2022-2024 but activity coverage expanded only 1.2x. 75% of AI market value concentrated in software/information tasks. Based on O*NET 29.1 and TAAFT dataset.

sources.title: AI's Systemic Impact on Labor Relations and Employment Structures
sources.excerpt: Industries with high volumes of structured, repetitive tasks face the sharpest near-term employment contractions.

sources.title: AI and Coder Employment: Compiling the Evidence
sources.excerpt: The coding occupations are overwhelmingly in the high exposure group according to both metrics, with more than 98 percent of coder employment in the highest quintiles.

sources.title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Board of Governors (Jeffrey S. Allen)
sources.excerpt: The SBU estimates an employment-weighted firm AI adoption rate of around 78 percent and an LLM adoption rate of about 54 percent. In this context, employment weighting approximates the share of the labor force working at firms that have adopted AI.

sources.title: The AI Jobs Transition Framework: Mapping AI's Near-Term Impact on Jobs
sources.excerpt: Jobs at high automation risk: gap 66.2 pp, 23.8% realized, 90.0% theoretical. Jobs that grow with AI: gap 49.7 pp, 22.7% realized, 72.4% theoretical. Jobs that will reorganize: gap 52.3 pp, 14.9% realized, 67.1% theoretical. Jobs with less immediate change: gap 21.0 pp, 6.4% realized, 27.4% theoretical. Across every job category, current usage lags behind the possible. Exposure alone is a weak predictor of immediate labor market pressure.

sources.title: You're (not) hired: Artificial intelligence and early career hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
sources.excerpt: At best, differences in monetary policy sensitivity can explain about one fourth of the regression-adjusted gap in employment, but monetary policy sensitivity does not appear to predict that AI-exposed firms would reduce their early career hiring activity more than others.

sources.title: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts
sources.excerpt: the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose sharply from its approximately 11% historical steady state to 16.8% in fiscal year 2025, a gain that has no precedent in 25 years of administrative records. ... the share of complaints containing AI-generated text has been rising monotonically from 1.0% in 2023 to 18.0% in early 2026.
